ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text: As shown in the figure, from a point $P$ outside the circle $\odot O$, rays $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to tangentially touch the circle $\odot O$ at points $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $\angle P = 50^\circ$. Point $C$ is on the minor arc $AB$. A tangent to circle $\odot O$ at point $C$ intersects $PA$ and $PB$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. What is the measure of $\angle DOE$ in degrees?
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
\textbf{Solution:} As shown in the diagram, connect OA, OC, OB,

since PA, PB, DE are tangential to the circle at points A, B, and E, respectively,

therefore, $OA \perp PA$,

$OB \perp PB$,

$OC \perp DE$,

since $\angle P = 50^\circ$,

therefore, $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - \angle P = 130^\circ$,

since $OA = OB = OC$,

therefore, DO bisects $\angle ADC$, EO bisects $\angle BEC$,

therefore, $\angle ADO = \angle CDO$,

$\angle CEO = \angle BEO$,

therefore, $\angle AOD = \angle COD$,

$\angle COE = \angle BOE$,

therefore, $\angle DOE = \angle COD + \angle COE = \frac{1}{2}\angle AOC + \frac{1}{2}\angle BOC = \frac{1}{2}\angle AOB = \boxed{65^\circ}$,

Reasoning: Still regard the three tangents PA, PB, DE as the lines on which the three sides of triangle PDE lie. Since the distances from O to these three tangents all equal the radius of the circle, O lies on the angle bisectors formed by these tangents; but from the position in the figure, O is not inside triangle PDE, but on the other side of DE, so O is the excenter of triangle PDE opposite vertex P. Thus OD and OE respectively bisect the exterior angles of triangle PDE at D and E on the side near the circle. method.method_draft: Treat the three tangent lines PA, PB, and DE as the sides of triangle PDE. From the image, D lies on the upper tangent PA, E lies on the lower tangent PB, and DE is the tangent at C, so the circle centered at O is tangent to all three sides of triangle PDE. Therefore O is the incenter of triangle PDE. Since OP? is not needed, use the incenter fact that OD and OE are internal angle bisectors of angles D and E of triangle PDE. The text gives the angle at P between the two tangents as 50°. In any triangle, the angle at the incenter between the bisectors to vertices D and E has the obtuse measure 90° + P/2; the smaller supplementary angle shown as ∠DOE in the diagram is 180° - (90° + 25°) = 65°.

method.method_draft: Use an analytic tangent-line model. From the image and text, A, C, and B are three tangency points on the same circle, with C between A and B on the minor arc; D is the intersection of the tangents at A and C, and E is the intersection of the tangents at C and B. Put O at the origin and take the circle to have radius 1. If a tangency point has polar angle t, its tangent line is x cos t + y sin t = 1. The intersection of tangents at angles u and v lies on the ray from O with direction angle (u+v)/2, because solving the two tangent equations gives a point proportional to (cos((u+v)/2), sin((u+v)/2)). Thus OD has direction halfway between the central directions of A and C, while OE has direction halfway between those of C and B. Hence ∠DOE = 1/2∠AOB. raw_record.original_question: As shown in the figure, from a point $P$ outside the circle $\odot O$, rays $PA$ and $PB$ are drawn to tangentially touch the circle $\odot O$ at points $A$ and $B$, respectively, with $\angle P = 50^\circ$. Point $C$ is on the minor arc $AB$. A tangent to circle $\odot O$ at point $C$ intersects $PA$ and $PB$ at points $D$ and $E$, respectively. What is the measure of $\angle DOE$ in degrees?
raw_record.answer:
\textbf{Solution:} As shown in the diagram, connect OA, OC, OB,

since PA, PB, DE are tangential to the circle at points A, B, and E, respectively,

therefore, $OA \perp PA$,

$OB \perp PB$,

$OC \perp DE$,

since $\angle P = 50^\circ$,

therefore, $\angle AOB = 180^\circ - \angle P = 130^\circ$,

since $OA = OB = OC$,

therefore, DO bisects $\angle ADC$, EO bisects $\angle BEC$,

therefore, $\angle ADO = \angle CDO$,

$\angle CEO = \angle BEO$,

therefore, $\angle AOD = \angle COD$,

$\angle COE = \angle BOE$,

therefore, $\angle DOE = \angle COD + \angle COE = \frac{1}{2}\angle AOC + \frac{1}{2}\angle BOC = \frac{1}{2}\angle AOB = \boxed{65^\circ}$,
raw_record.final_cot:
Image description: In the figure, point P is on the left, PA and PB are the upper and lower tangents drawn from P, tangent to the circle on the right at A and B respectively, and ∠P=50° is marked. The tangent drawn through point C near the left side of the circle intersects the upper tangent PA at D and the lower tangent PB at E; the small triangle PDE formed by D, E and P is on the left, while the center O of the circle and the circle are mainly located on the right side of line DE. OD and OE are drawn in the figure, and what is sought is the smaller angle ∠DOE formed at O by OD and OE.
Reasoning: Still regard the three tangents PA, PB, DE as the lines on which the three sides of triangle PDE lie. Since the distances from O to these three tangents all equal the radius of the circle, O lies on the angle bisectors formed by these tangents; but from the position in the figure, O is not inside triangle PDE, but on the other side of DE, so O is the excenter of triangle PDE opposite vertex P. Thus OD and OE respectively bisect the exterior angles of triangle PDE at D and E on the side near the circle. Let the interior angles of triangle PDE be ∠D=α and ∠E=β, then α+β=180°-∠P=180°-50°=130°. In triangle DOE, ∠ODE=(180°-α)/2, ∠DEO=(180°-β)/2, so ∠DOE=180°-[(180°-α)/2+(180°-β)/2]=(α+β)/2=130°/2=65°. Therefore the answer is 65°.
